question: What is the Java Collections Framework hierarchy?

options.text: Collection → List, Set, Queue; Map is separate (not a Collection)
Collection → List, Set, Map, Queue (all inherit from Collection)
Array → Collection → List, Set, Map
Object → Collection → List → ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap

explanation: The root interface is `Collection<E>` with subinterfaces: `List` (ordered, duplicates allowed), `Set` (no duplicates), `Queue`/`Deque` (FIFO/LIFO). `Map<K,V>` is a separate hierarchy — it does NOT extend Collection. Common: ArrayList, LinkedList (List); HashSet, TreeSet (Set); HashMap, TreeMap (Map); ArrayDeque (Queue/Deque).

question: What is the difference between `ArrayList` and `LinkedList`?

options.text: ArrayList: O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete at middle; LinkedList: O(n) random access, O(1) insert/delete at known node
ArrayList is thread-safe; LinkedList is not
LinkedList uses less memory than ArrayList
ArrayList allows null; LinkedList does not

explanation: ArrayList: backed by an array, O(1) get(index), O(n) add/remove in the middle (shifts elements), amortized O(1) add at end, better cache locality. LinkedList: doubly-linked nodes, O(1) add/remove at head/tail if you have the node reference, O(n) get(index). In practice, ArrayList outperforms LinkedList for most workloads due to cache efficiency — prefer ArrayList unless you specifically need O(1) head/tail operations.

question: What is the difference between `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeMap`?

options.text: HashMap: O(1) get/put, no order; LinkedHashMap: insertion-order or access-order; TreeMap: sorted by key, O(log n) operations
HashMap is synchronized; LinkedHashMap is not; TreeMap is read-only
TreeMap is fastest; HashMap is slowest
They are identical — just different naming conventions

explanation: HashMap: hash table, O(1) average get/put, no guaranteed order, allows one null key. LinkedHashMap: extends HashMap, maintains insertion order (or access order for LRU cache). TreeMap: Red-Black tree, keys sorted by natural order or Comparator, O(log n) for all operations — useful for range queries (`subMap`, `headMap`, `tailMap`).

question: How does HashMap work internally?

options.text: HashMap stores key-value pairs in a sorted array
HashMap uses an array of buckets; keys are hashed to a bucket index, stored in a linked list (or tree for large buckets) within that bucket
HashMap stores entries in a balanced binary search tree
HashMap uses a matrix of (key, value) pairs indexed by both dimensions

explanation: HashMap maintains an array (default 16 slots). To put a key: compute `hashCode()`, apply bit manipulation for index, store in that bucket. Collisions: Java 7 uses linked list per bucket; Java 8+ converts to TreeMap (red-black tree) when bucket has ≥ 8 entries (treeification). Load factor (default 0.75): when 75% full, the backing array doubles (rehashing). O(1) average; O(n) worst case with bad hash function.

question: What is the difference between `HashSet` and `TreeSet`?

options.text: HashSet: O(1) operations, no order; TreeSet: O(log n) operations, elements sorted by natural/Comparator order
HashSet allows duplicates; TreeSet does not
TreeSet is faster than HashSet for all operations
HashSet is thread-safe; TreeSet is not

explanation: HashSet: backed by HashMap (element is key, dummy value), O(1) add/contains/remove, no guaranteed iteration order. TreeSet: backed by TreeMap (NavigableSet), O(log n) all operations, elements always sorted. Use HashSet for fast membership checks; use TreeSet when you need sorted order or range operations (`headSet`, `tailSet`, `subSet`, `floor`, `ceiling`).

question: What is the difference between `Comparable` and `Comparator`?

options.text: Comparable defines the natural ordering within the class itself; Comparator is an external strategy for comparing two objects
Comparable is for sorting collections; Comparator is for sorting arrays
Comparator is built into the class; Comparable is external
They are identical — use whichever you prefer

explanation: `Comparable<T>` is implemented by the class to define its natural order: `compareTo(T other)`. `Comparator<T>` is a separate object providing an alternative or external comparison: `compare(T a, T b)`. Use Comparable when there is one obvious sort order; use Comparator for multiple orderings or when you can't modify the class. `Collections.sort(list, comparator)` and `list.sort(comparator)`.

question: What is `ConcurrentModificationException` and how do you avoid it?

options.text: An exception that occurs when two threads modify the same object
Thrown when a collection is structurally modified while iterating over it with an Iterator — avoid by using Iterator.remove(), CopyOnWriteArrayList, or collecting changes and applying after iteration
An exception thrown when a collection runs out of memory
Thrown only in multithreaded code when two threads access the same list

explanation: Most Java collections use a `modCount` counter. Iterators capture the count on creation and check it on each `next()` call — if modified externally, it throws ConcurrentModificationException (fail-fast). Solutions: (1) `iterator.remove()` — safe removal during iteration. (2) `removeIf(predicate)` on the collection. (3) Collect elements to remove, then removeAll after. (4) Use `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for concurrent use.

question: What is `Collections.unmodifiableList()` vs `List.of()` vs `List.copyOf()`?

options.text: They are identical — all create immutable lists
`unmodifiableList()`: a view that prevents modification but the backing list can change; `List.of()`: truly immutable, no nulls; `List.copyOf()`: immutable defensive copy of an existing collection
`List.of()` allows nulls; the others do not
`Collections.unmodifiableList()` is the modern replacement for `List.of()`

explanation: `Collections.unmodifiableList(list)` wraps a mutable list — the wrapper throws on mutation calls, but if the underlying list is modified directly, the view reflects that change. `List.of(1,2,3)` (Java 9): truly immutable, no nulls, fixed size. `List.copyOf(collection)` (Java 10): creates an immutable snapshot. For truly immutable collections, prefer `List.of()` or `List.copyOf()`.

question: When would you choose a `Deque` over a `Queue`?

options.text: When you need to add/remove from both ends (double-ended queue) — use ArrayDeque as a stack (push/pop) or queue (offer/poll)
Use Deque when the queue must be synchronized
Deque is only for LIFO; Queue is only for FIFO
Deque is slower than Queue — only use it for large datasets

explanation: `Deque` (double-ended queue) supports insertion/removal at both front and back. `ArrayDeque` is the most efficient general-purpose implementation — faster than `LinkedList` for both stack and queue use cases. Java docs recommend `ArrayDeque` over `Stack` (which is synchronized and extends Vector). Use `offerFirst`/`pollFirst` (stack) or `offerLast`/`pollFirst` (queue).

question: What is `PriorityQueue` and what ordering does it use?

options.text: PriorityQueue is a FIFO queue with automatic alphabetical ordering
PriorityQueue is a min-heap — the smallest element (by natural order or Comparator) is always at the head
PriorityQueue maintains insertion order with a priority number
PriorityQueue is a synchronized version of ArrayDeque

explanation: PriorityQueue is a heap-based priority queue. `poll()` always returns the smallest element (min-heap). For max-heap: `new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())`. O(log n) for offer/poll, O(1) for peek. Not thread-safe. Iteration order is undefined — only `poll()` guarantees priority order. Used for Dijkstra, task scheduling, top-K problems.

question: What is the initial capacity and load factor of HashMap, and how do they affect performance?

options.text: Initial capacity: 10, load factor: 0.5 — these cannot be changed

Initial capacity: 16, load factor: 0.75. When entries exceed capacity×loadFactor, the map rehashes (doubles capacity). Lower load factor = fewer collisions, more memory; higher = more collisions, less memory
Initial capacity: 100, load factor: 1.0 — the default is optimized for all cases
Initial capacity and load factor only matter for LinkedHashMap

explanation: Default: 16 buckets, 0.75 load factor. Rehash when size > 16×0.75=12. Rehashing doubles the array and re-distributes all entries — O(n) operation. If you know the final size, pre-size: `new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75 + 1)` to avoid rehashing. Lower load factor (e.g. 0.5) reduces collisions at cost of more memory; higher (e.g. 0.9) saves memory but increases collision rate.

question: What is `EnumMap` and `EnumSet` and when should you use them?

options.text: EnumMap and EnumSet are deprecated — use HashMap and HashSet instead

EnumMap: a Map implementation optimized for enum keys using an array (O(1), compact); EnumSet: a Set implementation for enum values using bit manipulation — both are faster than their general-purpose equivalents when keys are enums
EnumMap sorts entries by enum ordinal; EnumSet maintains insertion order
They are identical to HashMap/HashSet but restricted to String keys

explanation: EnumMap uses an array indexed by `enum.ordinal()` — O(1) and extremely compact, no hashing overhead. EnumSet uses a bit vector (single `long` for enums with ≤64 constants) — blazing fast, no boxing. Both maintain declaration order. Always use these when your key/element type is an enum — significant performance and memory advantage.

question: What is the difference between `Vector` and `ArrayList`, and should you use `Vector`?

options.text: Vector is the modern replacement for ArrayList
Vector is a legacy synchronized list (all methods synchronized) — use ArrayList for single-threaded code; use CopyOnWriteArrayList or synchronized wrappers for thread-safety instead
Vector is faster than ArrayList because it pre-allocates more memory
ArrayList is deprecated; Vector is the current standard

explanation: Vector predates the Collections Framework (Java 1.0). It synchronizes every method, causing unnecessary overhead in single-threaded code. ArrayList (Java 1.2) replaced it. For thread-safe lists: `Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>())` or `CopyOnWriteArrayList`. `Stack` (extends Vector) should be replaced with `ArrayDeque`. Don't use Vector in new code.

question: What is `WeakHashMap` and when would you use it?

options.text: WeakHashMap is a HashMap that allows null values
WeakHashMap holds weak references to keys — when a key is no longer referenced elsewhere, it is eligible for garbage collection and the entry is removed automatically
WeakHashMap is a slower HashMap used for testing purposes
WeakHashMap requires keys to implement WeakReference interface

explanation: WeakHashMap's keys are held via WeakReferences. When a key has no other strong references, the GC can reclaim it — the WeakHashMap entry is then removed. Use cases: caches where entries should be collected when the cached object is no longer used elsewhere (e.g. per-Class metadata, listener registries). Not thread-safe. Contrast with regular HashMap which prevents GC of its keys.

question: How do you correctly remove elements from a List while iterating?

options.text: Use a for-each loop and call list.remove(element) inside
Use Iterator and call iterator.remove(), or use list.removeIf(predicate), or iterate backwards with a traditional for loop
Use a for loop with an index and never skip indices
Collections cannot be modified during iteration — create a new list instead

explanation: For-each with `list.remove()` throws ConcurrentModificationException. Safe approaches: (1) `Iterator<E> it = list.iterator(); while(it.hasNext()) { if(condition) it.remove(); }` (2) `list.removeIf(e -> condition)` — cleanest. (3) Traditional for loop iterating backwards: `for(int i=list.size()-1; i>=0; i--) { if(condition) list.remove(i); }` — safe because removals don't affect unvisited indices.

question: What is `Map.getOrDefault()`, `Map.computeIfAbsent()`, and `Map.merge()` used for?

options.text: They are deprecated — use get() and put() for all Map operations
getOrDefault: get with fallback; computeIfAbsent: lazy compute and cache; merge: combine existing value with new value — all reduce boilerplate for common Map patterns
They are used only with ConcurrentHashMap
computeIfAbsent and merge only work with Integer values

explanation: `getOrDefault(key, default)`: returns value or default without null-check. `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> value)`: if key absent, computes and puts value — perfect for `Map<String, List<>>` grouping. `merge(key, value, (old,new) -> combined)`: if key absent puts value; if present applies merge function — perfect for frequency counting: `map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)`.

question: What is the difference between `Arrays.asList()` and `List.of()`?

options.text: They are identical — both return an immutable fixed-size list
`Arrays.asList()`: fixed-size but mutable (set() works, add/remove throw); backed by the array — changes to the array reflect in the list. `List.of()`: fully immutable, no nulls allowed
`List.of()` is backed by an array; `Arrays.asList()` is backed by a LinkedList
`Arrays.asList()` is deprecated; use `List.of()` for all cases

explanation: `Arrays.asList(arr)` returns a fixed-size List backed by the original array — `set()` works and changes are reflected in the array, but `add()`/`remove()` throw UnsupportedOperationException. Allows null. `List.of(1,2,3)` (Java 9): fully immutable — set/add/remove all throw, null elements throw NullPointerException. Choose `List.of()` for truly immutable collections.

question: What is `IdentityHashMap` and when would you use it?

options.text: IdentityHashMap uses == for key comparison instead of equals()
IdentityHashMap is a HashMap where keys must implement an Identity interface
IdentityHashMap is a WeakHashMap with identity-based comparison
IdentityHashMap requires keys to be Strings

explanation: `IdentityHashMap` uses reference equality (`==`) and `System.identityHashCode()` for keys instead of `equals()`/`hashCode()`. Two distinct objects with equal content are treated as different keys. Use cases: object graph serialization (tracking visited objects to detect cycles), proxy caches keyed by identity, compiler symbol tables.

question: What is `Collections.sort()` vs `List.sort()` vs `Arrays.sort()`?

options.text: Collections.sort() is for arrays; Arrays.sort() is for lists

Collections.sort(list): sorts a List, delegates to list.sort() since Java 8. List.sort(comparator): instance method. Arrays.sort(array): sorts primitive arrays (dual-pivot quicksort) or Object arrays (Timsort). All are O(n log n).
Arrays.sort() is slower — always prefer Collections.sort()
They use different algorithms and cannot be used interchangeably

explanation: `Collections.sort(list)` and `list.sort(null)` are equivalent since Java 8 — both use Timsort (O(n log n), stable). `Arrays.sort(int[])` uses dual-pivot quicksort (not stable, faster for primitives). `Arrays.sort(Object[])` uses Timsort (stable). For parallel sorting of large arrays: `Arrays.parallelSort()` uses fork/join. Prefer `list.sort(comparator)` for readability.

question: What is `ConcurrentHashMap` and how does it differ from `Collections.synchronizedMap()`?

options.text: They are identical — both lock the entire map on every operation

ConcurrentHashMap uses segment/bucket-level locking (allows concurrent reads and some concurrent writes); synchronizedMap locks the entire map for every operation — ConcurrentHashMap is much more performant under concurrent access
synchronizedMap is more modern; ConcurrentHashMap is legacy
ConcurrentHashMap does not support null keys; synchronizedMap does

explanation: `synchronizedMap` wraps a map with a single mutex — every read and write is serialized. `ConcurrentHashMap` (Java 5+): reads are lock-free; writes use bucket-level CAS/synchronized (Java 8: node-level locking), enabling true concurrent reads and high write concurrency. Also supports atomic operations: `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`. Does not allow null keys or values.

question: What is the difference between `Iterator` and `ListIterator`?

options.text: Iterator is for forward-only traversal; ListIterator is for Lists only and supports bidirectional traversal, modification, and index access
ListIterator is the old API; Iterator is the modern replacement
Iterator supports modification; ListIterator is read-only
They are identical — ListIterator just has a longer name

explanation: `Iterator`: forward-only, works on any Iterable (`hasNext()`, `next()`, `remove()`). `ListIterator` (extends Iterator): works only on Lists, supports bidirectional traversal (`hasPrevious()`, `previous()`), modification (`set()`, `add()`), and index queries (`nextIndex()`, `previousIndex()`). Use `list.listIterator()` to get one.

question: What does `Collections.frequency()`, `Collections.disjoint()`, and `Collections.nCopies()` do?

options.text: These methods do not exist in the Collections class
`frequency(collection, obj)`: count occurrences; `disjoint(c1, c2)`: true if no common elements; `nCopies(n, obj)`: immutable list of n copies of obj
`frequency()` returns the most frequent element; `disjoint()` returns duplicate-free version; `nCopies()` creates a synchronized list
They are only available in Java 11+

explanation: Useful utility methods: `Collections.frequency(list, "a")` — counts how many times "a" appears. `Collections.disjoint(set1, set2)` — true if they share no elements (intersection is empty). `Collections.nCopies(3, "x")` — returns `["x", "x", "x"]` as an immutable list, useful for initializing or filling collections.

question: What is `NavigableMap` and what operations does it add over `SortedMap`?

options.text: NavigableMap is just a renamed SortedMap — they have the same methods
NavigableMap extends SortedMap with navigation methods: floor, ceiling, lower, higher, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, and descendingMap
NavigableMap is a concurrent version of SortedMap
NavigableMap supports range queries; SortedMap does not

explanation: `SortedMap` provides `firstKey()`, `lastKey()`, `headMap()`, `tailMap()`, `subMap()`. `NavigableMap` (extends SortedMap, implemented by TreeMap) adds: `floor(k)` (greatest key ≤ k), `ceiling(k)` (least key ≥ k), `lower(k)` (strictly <), `higher(k)` (strictly >), `pollFirstEntry()`, `pollLastEntry()`, `descendingMap()`. Very useful for interval lookups and ordered event processing.

question: What is `ArrayDeque` and why is it preferred over `Stack` and `LinkedList` as a stack/queue?

options.text: ArrayDeque is slower — use Stack for stacks and LinkedList for queues
ArrayDeque uses a resizable array with no per-element overhead — faster than LinkedList (cache locality) and unsynchronized unlike Stack
ArrayDeque is synchronized; Stack and LinkedList are not
ArrayDeque only supports FIFO; it cannot be used as a stack

explanation: `Stack` is synchronized (unnecessary overhead) and extends `Vector` (legacy). `LinkedList` has per-node memory overhead and poor cache performance. `ArrayDeque` (circular buffer backed by array): no synchronization overhead, excellent cache locality, amortized O(1) for all deque operations. Java docs explicitly recommend `ArrayDeque` over `Stack`. Use `push`/`pop` for stack semantics, `offer`/`poll` for queue.

question: How would you find the duplicate elements in a List efficiently?

options.text: Sort the list and check adjacent elements — O(n log n)
Use a HashSet: iterate the list, add each element to the set — elements that return false from add() are duplicates. O(n) time, O(n) space
Compare every element to every other element — O(n²)
Use Collections.frequency() for each element — O(n²)

explanation: Optimal approach: `Set<T> seen = new HashSet<>(); Set<T> dups = new HashSet<>(); for(T e : list) { if(!seen.add(e)) dups.add(e); }` — O(n) time, O(n) space. `Set.add()` returns false if the element was already present. Alternatively: `list.stream().filter(e -> Collections.frequency(list, e) > 1).collect(toSet())` — simpler but O(n²).
